**The Last Letter**

I found it in the attic, folded neatly between the dusty shelves of my grandfather’s books. The paper was yellowed with age, the edges slightly frayed, as if it had been tucked away for decades. I unfolded it carefully, my fingers trembling slightly.

*Dearest [Name],*

*I write to you from a place I never thought I’d be. The war has taken everything—our home, our lives, our futures. But I must tell you this: I am alive. I am here, in this strange, unfamiliar land, where the air smells different and the people speak in hushed tones. I have no money, no family, and no hope. But I have you.*

*I don’t know how to reach you. The letters I sent were lost, swallowed by the chaos. But I will keep writing, even if no one reads them. I will keep hoping that one day, you will find this and know that I am still here.*

*Please, [Name], don’t forget me. Don’t let this war erase us completely. I love you. Always.*

*— [His Name]*

I sat there, the words pressing into my chest like a weight. My grandfather had never spoken of this war, never mentioned the letters he’d sent or received. But here it was, proof of a life I had never known.

I thought of the way he’d always smile when he talked about his youth, the way he’d tell stories of a time before the world had changed. Now, I understood. He had been gone for years, fighting in a war that had left him broken, but not forgotten.

I refolded the letter carefully, my hands steadying. I would keep it. I would remember. And one day, I would tell my own children about the man who had loved me before I was born.

Because some things, no matter how long they’ve been buried, never truly die.
